A hard low shaft drives in from behind the wax sheets, passing clean through sealed honey so every cup burns molten gold, and one small curl of dropped wax catches the beam and glows hot apricot against deep emerald shade.

Late almost-level sun enters from the left side past the trunk, laying one long apricot stripe down the bark and rimming the overlapping wax sheets in hot gold, while a bead of pine resin plugging a cracked cup holds the light like a lit ember.

Light bounces up off a brimming pool of spilt honey on the footing and throws amber from below onto the undersides of every hanging sheet, against the cool teal of the canopy shadow above, and a beetle drunk on the drip sits lit from beneath like a small lamp.

The canopy overhead burns such a saturated hot green that the whole scene runs in green light, and the honey is the single warm note — pooling vivid apricot on the footing, holding amber where it runs along the wood grain.

One narrow shaft through a knothole strikes the wax sheets edge-on so their wavy lower hems glow rose-gold and their broad faces stay cool cream, and the same shaft catches a single amber drop mid-fall, frozen in the beam like a bead of trapped sun.

Smoke drifts slowly across the shaft from the left, turning the whole beam visible and grainy-gold, everything beyond it going hazy apricot while the near wax sheets stay sharp-edged and molten, and a snail crossing the full width of the footing moves through three distinct light zones.

The sky beyond the trunk goes bright white-gold so the wax sheets, and everything close to the wood, read as warm amber silhouettes against a blazing apricot ground, and one small crescent of honey still clinging to a broken edge burns nearly translucent at its rim.

Rain just stopped: every wet bark surface throws a hard bright highlight in ember-orange, and the saturated canopy behind it answers in deep moss-green, so the whole picture flickers between two vivid poles and one boot-print in the spilt honey below mirrors the sky in miniature.

A honey sheet lifted clear into the gap in the canopy catches direct sun straight through itself, its whole face turning one solid wall of molten gold with the six-sided cup pattern standing as a fine amber lattice against it, and the hand holding it glows through at the fingers.

Light arrives thick with hanging pollen, the whole air turned to warm amber haze, and the wax sheets catch it from the left side so their faces go deep apricot while the moss on the bark behind them stays saturated emerald and untouched by the warmth.

A break in the leaves throws one small burning patch of direct sun onto a single wax sheet and leaves the rest of the hanging layers in cool teal shade, so that one lit sheet sings molten amber in a frame of cold colour, and a moth has already found the warm spot.

Honey pours off a broken sheet edge and the shaft of light strikes it straight through its full length, so the pour turns to a column of liquid amber fire against the deep emerald shadow behind the trunk, and the footing below mirrors it in a bright gold splash.

The trunk reads as a warm dark silhouette against a sky gone blazing white-gold beyond it, and the wax sheets hanging from the limb above are caught in that backlight so their edges rim in apricot and their bellies stay cool blue-grey where the trunk's shadow falls across them.

Late sun from one side comes in almost level under the canopy and passes through a lifted honey sheet before it hits the bark, so the bark wears a faint warm gold cast and every surface beyond the sheet stands in deep teal cool shadow, unwarmed and watching.

Light bouncing up off a spilt honey pool floods the scene from below in amber, gilding the undersides of every wax sheet and throwing warm light against the otherwise cool moss-green bark above, and a woodlouse near the pool's edge crosses a boundary between gold and green in four small steps.

One narrow shaft comes through a gap behind the wax and catches the sheets front-on, so the honey in every sealed cup lights to molten amber and the pale wax walls between them stay cream, setting two vivid colours side by side all across the sheet face.

Smoke drifts into the shaft from the right and the beam goes thick and apricot-gold, while the wax sheets on the far side of it shift to warm amber seen through haze, and the footing near the smoke source shines clear ember-orange where the full beam still strikes the honey pool.

The canopy gap above the nest is wide enough to throw a column of hot gold light straight down from overhead, so the tops of the wax sheets burn apricot and their lower wavy hems hang in the cool indigo of the deep shade below, the two colours sharing each sheet's length.

Almost-level late sun enters from the right and passes through a bee-wing held out to balance, so one brief wing turns translucent amber-gold before the light continues onto the wax and streaks it in a long hot apricot bar against the deep emerald bark shadow behind.

The sky beyond the trunk turns such a bright white-gold that the wax sheets hanging this side of it are fully backlit, their sealed cups going amber-translucent at the edges and cream at their thick centres, and the bark of the trunk itself reads as a rich deep teal against that brightness.

Light comes in low through a gap in the leaves from the left side, strikes a hanging wax sheet from behind, and every sealed cup of honey ignites to molten gold while the air in front of the sheet stays in saturated emerald canopy-cool, the two colours cut hard at the wax face.

A single break in the canopy drops one burning column of direct sun onto the footing where honey has pooled, and from that pool amber light bounces up and coats the undersides of every sheet and the moss on the bark above in warm gold, against the teal shade beyond the column's edge.

The whole canopy above has gone to hot saturated green and the scene runs in that green light, and the honey running down the wood is the only warmth — a narrow amber path lit from within against the surrounding moss-green, and a small glass-clear drop at its tip holds both colours at once.

Pollen hangs so thick in the beam from the left that the light arrives amber before it even touches the wax, and the wax sheets it reaches glow a deep molten gold while the bark beyond the beam stays in the vivid emerald of the canopy shadow, cool and still.

Rain just ended and the bark is wet all over: a shaft coming in low from the right strikes the wet surface and throws a hard ember-orange highlight along every grain and ridge, while the wax sheets above it catch the same shaft through their lower hems, rimming them in rose-gold above the hot bark below.
